title: Review: MaraBela Sparkling Tea Wild Verbena
summary:
Packaged in a 750ml wine bottle with a Champagne style cork, you could be forgiven for assuming MaraBela was a new sparkling wine, albeit perhaps with a new age bent. The post Review: MaraBela Sparkling Tea Wild Verbena appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Packaged in a 750ml wine bottle with a Champagne style cork, you could be forgiven for assuming MaraBela was a new sparkling wine, albeit perhaps with a new age bent. It’s not, though, it’s tea: sparkling tea, specifically, designed as a non-alcoholic alternative to a traditional bottle of bubbly.

Per the brand:

MaraBela wasn’t created in response to trend data. As an athlete who regularly goes through periods without alcohol, Co-Founder Jesús Martínez Bujanda wanted something he genuinely enjoyed at the table when he wasn’t drinking. But this new research does reinforce the family’s decision to create a dry, 0.0% sparkling tea built around complexity, ritual and food.

At 12 calories per serving, it’s perhaps the most harmless beverage you can enjoy short of a glass of water. Let’s give it a try.

MaraBela Sparkling Tea Wild Verbena Review

On the nose, the beverage is quite innocuous, barely there as it lingers in glass. Time helps the tea’s herbaceous qualities come to the fore, the product offering a clear mix of black tea leaf and fresh herbs, though it never approaches anything overwhelming, remaining quite mild long after it’s been poured.

The palate offers a clearer, slightly stronger character that shows off a mix of red berries — strawberry and raspberry notes predominant. In time, more floral notes begin to dominate on the tongue, along with a lemon peel quality that finally evokes the verbena in the recipe. The finish is quite bright and very refreshing: You could easily polish off a bottle of this at dinner without thinking twice. (Though my recommendation is to serve it over ice, to help keep it cold.)

A curious and fun N/A alternative to wine, it’s not quite the same as drinking a dealcoholized sparkling wine (of which there are many good options), but it’s definitely a more elegant and nuanced option than, say, a bottle of Martinelli’s.

A- / $20

title: Review: Bulleit ’87
summary:
Blending bourbon and rye used to be a wild novelty, but now it’s surprisingly commonplace, perhaps due to the runaway success of High West’s Bourye, which has become an annually released, prized commodity among those in the know. The latest to jump into the blending game is Bulleit, whose new Bulleit ’87 is in some…

The post Review: Bulleit ’87 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Blending bourbon and rye used to be a wild novelty, but now it’s surprisingly commonplace, perhaps due to the runaway success of High West’s Bourye, which has become an annually released, prized commodity among those in the know.

The latest to jump into the blending game is Bulleit, whose new Bulleit ’87 is in some ways a throwback to the Reagan years. While the brand would take years to reach prominence, it was actually launched in 1987, well before the bourbon boom was on anyone’s radar.

This is a new core expression (the first since 2011) entering the permanent lineup, blending standard Bulleit Bourbon (from Kentucky) and Bulleit 95 Rye (from Indiana) in unstated proportions. Both the bourbon and rye are aged for at least four years, “finished separately in their original barrels with toasted American oak and French oak staves for four to six weeks, then blended together and bottled in Shelbyville, Kentucky.”

Let’s dive in.

Bulleit ’87 Review

My primitive thoughts on the brand from nearly 20 years ago aside, today’s Bulleit isn’t known for being an aggressive whiskey, and ’87 is probably the softest expression in the Bulleit arsenal to date. The nose is quite buttery, with immediate shortbread overtones, though a low-level smokiness slowly comes into view with time in glass. Rye spice elements make an appearance, with a whiff of cherry pits later. Cloves linger.

The palate again kicks off as quite soft and understated, more brown butter than fresh, some popcorn, caramel, and a dusting of spice. The whiskey never really picks up from there, as fruitier elements come into the picture — baked apples, sugared pears, and just a hint of golden raisins on the back end. As is the case with the nose, the rye-driven spice doesn’t appear much at all until the finish begins to near, with cinnamon and clove notes, punctuated with the occasional plump red berry, pop into the fore. None of it really lasts, though, the finish returning to those buttery, biscuity notes, with Bulleit ’87 ultimately fading from view with the impression of a cookie. A whiskeyish cookie, but emphasis on the latter.

The bottle’s a mixer, but a solid and versatile one, to the point where it feels like that was entirely the point in its creation. The name may confuse everyone who sips it. In a cocktail — of which I’ve had a few — the idea should come across with ease.

90 proof.

B+ / $30 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: 2024 Sankt Pauls Pinot Grigio Sudtirol Aldo Adige appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Alto Adige pinot grigio (Santa Margherita generally excepted) offers the drinker the opportunity to experience this wine without the expected trappings that have become typical of today’s production. Rather than overtly fruity and vaguely sweet, Sankt Pauls’ expression is layered and quite dry, an exploration of terroir instead of the orchard.

Crisp and mineral-driven on the palate, this wine from Kellerei St. Pauls takes its gentle, turned earth kickoff, touched just so with a spritz of oxidized white wine vinegar which only amplifies the dryness of the wine. More classic pinot grigio notes emerge from there: Melon mixed with lighter pineapple notes, finishing on a spray of white flowers, both fresh and dried. It’s a wine that’s versatile, approachable, and
restrained all at once — a crowd-pleaser with nuance that hits well above its price band.

A- / $29

title: Review: Penelope Founders Reserve Bourbon 13, Conundrum Rye 12, and Cigar Sessions Chapter 2
summary:
There is more than one way to make a whiskey worth talking about. Time can transform a spirit as it interacts with oak over the course of years. Selecting and blending barrels can bring individual components together to create something greater than the sum of their parts. And sometimes, the goal is not simply to…

The post Review: Penelope Founders Reserve Bourbon 13, Conundrum Rye 12, and Cigar Sessions Chapter 2 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
There is more than one way to make a whiskey worth talking about. Time can transform a spirit as it interacts with oak over the course of years. Selecting and blending barrels can bring individual components together to create something greater than the sum of their parts. And sometimes, the goal is not simply to create a whiskey that stands on its own, but one designed to complement an entirely different experience.

Penelope’s 2026 releases offer an opportunity to explore these different approaches to whiskey making. The Estate Collection brings together Founders Reserve Bourbon 13 Years Old , and Conundrum Rye 12 Years Old, while Cigar Sessions Chapter 02 American Whiskey takes a different approach, with an emphasis on the cigar-pairing experience. Each release has its own purpose, giving us three different perspectives on what goes into making a memorable whiskey. Let’s take a closer look at each release and see how Penelope brought its vision to life.

Penelope Estate Collection Conundrum Rye 12 Years Old Review

Batch No. 26-2001 of the Penelope Estate Collection was distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana, from a mashbill of 95% rye and 5% malted barley. It also marks the oldest rye whiskey Penelope has released to date. The distillate entered barrels at 120 proof, and the whiskey was bottled without chill filtration.

The nose opens with mulled, unfiltered apple cider, with the apple taking precedence while the mulling spices play a supporting role. As the initial cider notes recede, Red Twizzlers bring a waxy red fruit quality. Spearmint gum makes an appearance, as expected from an MGP 95/5 rye, though the mint is exceptionally faint. Given more time in the glass, Butterfinger candy bar filling takes over, with the chocolate nowhere to be found and the peanut butter candy center taking the spotlight. I’m a fan of the bright, herbaceous profile often associated with MGP 95/5 rye, but I thoroughly enjoy this departure from that style. Oak takes a more prominent role here without becoming overly tannic. The nose suggests a palate with considerable concentration.

The first sip delivers a strong dose of Hawaiian Punch Fruit Juicy Red. I’m not sure I’ve encountered such an intense red fruit note in an Indiana-distilled 95/5 rye, and I like it. As the fruit subsides, peppermint candy develops, though with less sweetness than the little red-and-white discs. Blue raspberry candy follows through the mid-palate before giving way to clove. As the nose suggests, the palate is dense and full, with ample sweetness that stops short of becoming cloying.

Honey cough drops lead the finish, followed by mild cinnamon gum and a savory combination of black pepper and bacon with a pepper-crusted edge.

I’m a big fan of rye whiskey, in large part because of the range of profiles it can offer. The herbal notes commonly associated with MGP 95/5 rye can be polarizing, but they’re a major part of what I enjoy about the style. Penelope Estate Collection Batch No. 26-2001 presents an interesting departure from expectations, with age and oak taking precedence over the profile many enthusiasts associate with this mashbill. For drinkers who believe they already know what MGP 95/5 rye has to offer, this release provides a welcome reason to reconsider those assumptions. 101.5 proof. A- / $85

Penelope Cigar Sessions Chapter 02 American Whiskey Review

Like Cigar Sessions Chapter 01, Chapter 02 combines bourbon, American single malt, and light whiskey distilled by MGP in Lawrenceburg, Indiana. The blend has a derived mashbill of 69% corn, 19% rye, and 12% malted barley, with bourbon accounting for the largest share. Each component was aged for at least six years. Penelope partnered with master cigar blenders Alec Bradley to develop a whiskey intended to pair with a medium- to full-bodied cigar. As a non-smoker, I’m evaluating Chapter 02 on its own, without the intended cigar pairing.

The nose opens with mild maple fudge, offering creamy maple sweetness without becoming excessive. Freshly sharpened No. 2 pencils add a touch of wood and graphite, followed by pizzelle and the honeyed sweetness of Bit-O-Honey candy. The result is a mildly sweet, bready nose that’s enjoyable, if not particularly elaborate.

Cow Tale candy leads the palate, bringing caramel and vanilla with a touch of nutmeg. The mid-palate moves toward malty Ovaltine and Grape-Nuts cereal, with an exceptionally memorable oily mouthfeel.

The finish brings oatmeal with brown sugar and nutmeg, followed by walnut. The flavors remain in keeping with the cereal, candy, and baking spice notes found earlier in the tasting.

Chapter 02 is a worthwhile step up from Chapter 01, particularly when evaluated without a cigar. It stands on its own more successfully, offering enough flavor and a pleasingly oily mouthfeel to make the whiskey enjoyable apart from its intended pairing. The profile should also appeal to more drinkers than its predecessor, making Chapter 02 the more approachable of the two releases for those who plan to enjoy the whiskey on its own. 117.4 proof. B+ / $80 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Penelope Estate Collection Founders Reserve Bourbon 13 Years Old (2026) Review

Founders Reserve is distilled by MGP from a mashbill of 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley. The batch identifications, 12L03K09BNL and 12L04L01BNL, indicate that the respective components entered barrels at 120 proof on December 3 and 4, 2012. The whiskey matured for more than 13 years in barrels sourced from Independent Stave Company, resting on floors 6 and 1 of Warehouse E. The 2025 Founders Reserve 13 Year Old release was distilled in Kentucky.

The nose opens with gingersnaps and orange bitters, bringing spice and citrus to the forefront before giving way to crème brûlée and toasted coconut. It’s an enjoyable combination, and the oak influence is less pronounced than I anticipated from a whiskey of this age. With more time in the glass, the gingersnap and orange bitters notes become increasingly prominent, while the sweetness gradually recedes.

Brown butter and toasted walnut lead the palate, followed by cacao nibs and clove through the mid-palate. Although the nose suggests less oak influence than expected, the palate introduces an astringent oak quality that doesn’t suit my preferences. The mouthfeel is somewhat drying, and that sensation detracts from the experience.

Chocolate stout and fresh ginger arrive on the finish, followed by burnt brown sugar and additional walnut. The astringency returns here, becoming increasingly drying as the finish progresses.

Taste is subjective, and I can see this profile appealing to drinkers who favor oak-forward bourbon. For me, however, the astringency detracts from an otherwise enjoyable nose and an interesting combination of flavors. At $200, I struggle to justify the price based on what’s in the glass. Even at $50, this isn’t a bottle I’d choose to purchase. Those who prefer more oak influence may find more to appreciate, but I don’t believe this release delivers $200 worth of enjoyment, even with its age statement. 101.4 proof. B / $200 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

Here’s a look at two new releases. 2023 One Stone Cabernet Sauvignon Paso Robles Review The 2023 edition of this screw-capped cabernet defies expectations, offering moderated sweetness and varietal authenticity, notes of currants tempered with oak, rhubarb, and a dash of vanilla, finishing…

The post Review: One Stone 2023 Cabernet Sauvignon and 2025 Rose of Pinot Noir appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Ancient Peaks offshoot One Stone continues to surprise with its ultra-value wines. Here’s a look at two new releases.

2023 One Stone Cabernet Sauvignon Paso Robles Review

The 2023 edition of this screw-capped cabernet defies expectations, offering moderated sweetness and varietal authenticity, notes of currants tempered with oak, rhubarb, and a dash of vanilla, finishing with a touch of spicy licorice. Notes of nutmeg cling to the finish, which echoes the gently tannic currants visible from the start, eventually followed by touches of dark chocolate. It’s all quite gentle and approachable from start to finish, less earthy than the 2021 bottling and more immediately approachable — great in its own, different way. Seems like a fine way to go at things to me. Again, a great value. A- / $20

2025 One Stone Rose of Pinot Noir Central Coast

A wholly approachable, springtime rose, this wine charges forward with bold notes of strawberry tempered by orange blossoms, lemon curd, and sugar cookie dough, all whipped into a swirl that’s topped with torn petals of white flowers. It’s not exactly a complicated wine, and it really doesn’t need to be: Bright acidity and a hint of saline give the experience even more of a lift, with mere touches of orange peel lingering on the finish. A- / $18

title: Review: Powers Irish Rye
summary:
While Irish whiskey is typically crafted from a blend of grains — predominantly barley — with this bottling Powers takes things in an unusual direction. As the name suggests, this is a 100% rye whiskey, column distilled at Midleton and aged for 4 to 5 years in a mix of virgin American oak, first-fill, and…

The post Review: Powers Irish Rye appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
While Irish whiskey is typically crafted from a blend of grains — predominantly barley — with this bottling Powers takes things in an unusual direction. As the name suggests, this is a 100% rye whiskey, column distilled at Midleton and aged for 4 to 5 years in a mix of virgin American oak, first-fill, and second-fill casks.

Let’s dig in.

Powers Irish Rye Review

This whiskey is immediately interesting for the way it effectively blends the styles of a classic Irish whiskey with a spicy, American style rye. The nose is quite hearty, in contrast to the often wispy, ephemeral Irish style, a mix of bracing herbs, sweeter baking spice, and honeyed cereal grains all hit the nose together. There’s also more of a pure wood influence here than in a traditional Irish, with notes of almond and apple wood lingering with time in glass.

The palate does not change the script much, kicking off with notes of almond and sesame, then a layer of melon, more cantaloupe than honeydew. The whiskey turns rather grassy from that point, quite fresh with overtones of lemon and bright baking spices. Notes of pastry cream infused with cinnamon offer a boldly dessert-like midpalate, though the sweetness is moderated. The experience oscillates — some herbaceousness, some sweeter tones, then back again — until it lands on the finish with the essence of almond croissants.

All told, it’s a wholly atypical Irish whiskey — and, perhaps, all the better for it.

86.4 proof.

A- / $35 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Waterdrop Instant Hot and Cold Countertop Water Filter Dispenser CT01
summary:
Isn’t it about high time we had space-saving on-demand convenience for fetching filtered hot or cold water at home with a touch of a button? Hadn’t thought of it? Probably not top of mind given the existing options in the water category. Refrigerators come with spouts for cold water, and electric kettles boil water in…

The post Review: Waterdrop Instant Hot and Cold Countertop Water Filter Dispenser CT01 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Isn’t it about high time we had space-saving on-demand convenience for fetching filtered hot or cold water at home with a touch of a button? Hadn’t thought of it? Probably not top of mind given the existing options in the water category. Refrigerators come with spouts for cold water, and electric kettles boil water in under a minute with a push of a button, so there’s no shortage of gadgets that attach to your faucet for filtration. But, indeed, the time has come for a standalone all-in-one countertop unit to continue to narrow that convenience gap. 

Let’s consider today’s candidate from Waterdrop, well regarded for their filtration systems, who now offers the CT01 Instant Hot & Cold Countertop Water Filter System. It weighs about 15 lbs, stands 14.44″ × 10.61″ × 13.43 with a detachable 1.32 gallon tank to forego plumbing installation and just plugs into any outlet of your choice. (We’re no strangers to countertop filtration systems or Waterdrop, see our 2025 review of their reverse osmosis filter dispenser.)

The device applies an “Advanced 6-Stage Filtration System” that “reduces chlorine, rust, and other impurities while retaining beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium.” You get hot or cold water “in seconds” with just a touch of various buttons offering personalized control and customization of temperature and volume. The 1.32-gallon container holds the equivalent of “28 × 6 oz cups” or in more relatable everyday metrics, about 6 to 10 commonly sized refillable water bottles. 

One can’t consider convenience without considering setup and maintenance, and, especially when it comes to “smart” things, how immune they are to user error. On balance, you only need to plug this into the wall to operate; it does not require plumbing to attach to your faucet or pipes. Which means the water supply is wholly dependent on you filling it up. It’s a decent trade off in my mind. 

The “touch-button” proposition is a bit more nuanced. Yes, you just have to press a couple of shiny little icons to fill your cup. But those shiny little icons need introductions about what they do and more critically, what you should not do. As a re-emerging luddite that admits knobs and dials are increasingly more appealing, trying to decipher how to manage the cute little figures in the proper order took embarrassingly longer than I care to admit. I was nervous a careless swipe would lead to water all over the floor or a malfunction. I took time to read the manual, and when I still didn’t trust myself, I checked the website to reach customer support. I was happy to see they had a Chat option, and was disappointed when no chat person or bot was home. I switched to old fashioned email to customer service. Unfortunately I am still waiting for a response, but with some steady pacing and careful repeat studying of the manual, I managed to figure out what the various icons were and what it means when one of them flashes or disappears. 

Post-testing inertia has left this temporary unit somewhat semi-permanently situated on our countertop. Increasingly our household has become spoiled with shaving minutes/seconds of the day to access instant hot or cold water. I knew I was a convert when I went to turn on our electric kettle and thought: Wait, there is already hot water just a few feet away, right now. I placed a mug with a tea bag under the dispenser and touched a few little pictures and walked away while the process completed. 

The long and short of it is that the product delivers on its promises. Water is clean tasting (an oxymoronic assessment, I know), and the convenience is all there. And it’s all packaged in a very sleek contraption to boot (think Eve from Wall-E). The filter lasts through 300 gallons before replacement is needed, though note that both the side and lower tanks are recommended to be emptied every few days. That is a chore I can definitely handle.  

A- / $220 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: New Riff Wheated Bourbon 6 Years Old
summary:
Based in Newport, Kentucky — just a stone’s throw from the Ohio River, and right across from Cincinnati — New Riff has never been averse to playing with mash bills and grain types. Its latest special release whiskey honors that ethos, delivering a wheated bourbon from a notably uncommon recipe: 65% corn 18% floor-malted wheat…

The post Review: New Riff Wheated Bourbon 6 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Based in Newport, Kentucky — just a stone’s throw from the Ohio River, and right across from Cincinnati — New Riff has never been averse to playing with mash bills and grain types. Its latest special release whiskey honors that ethos, delivering a wheated bourbon from a notably uncommon recipe:

  • 65% corn
  • 18% floor-malted wheat
  • 10% unmalted wheat
  • 7% dark wheat

According to a distillery representative, that grain bill takes inspiration from beer and allowed production staff to flex their deep brewing experience. New Riff is no stranger to beer-inspired whiskeys, also exemplified by a relatively recent “Duet” collab with Rhinegeist Brewery.

This new wheated bourbon was made from the aforementioned mash bill, then aged for six years. It’s presented as a bottled-in-bond product and — as with virtually all New Riff whiskeys — is presented without chill filtration. But getting your hands on a bottle may require jumping through a few minor hoops. This bottling is the newest product exclusive to New Riff’s Whiskey Club. It’s free to join, though releases are available for distillery pickup only.

Let’s see how it tastes.

New Riff Wheated Bourbon 6 Years Old Review

The nose starts off with ample candied fruit, specifically lemon drops and watermelon Jolly Rancher. At first, it’s bright and slightly tart, though aromas get richer, sweeter, oakier, and more grain-forward with a bit more time in the glass. (Yes, it evolves quite a bit!) Malt syrup and saltwater taffy are up next, followed by Weetabix cereal, which together bring a lightly sweet grain quality where the wheat really punches through in several forms. Those early fruit candy notes are almost gone after a few minutes, replaced (it seems) by lemongrass. Cocoa powder and cinnamon round out a nose that feels adjacent to New Riff’s classic bourbon profile with a touch more grain.

Even for a standard bottled-in-bond, this hits first as an easy sipper, drinking noticeably below proof. That’s not necessarily a knock against. Indeed, that first taste is lovely, like a fusion of those lemon drops and the milk leftover from a bowl of Cracklin’ Oat Bran. Toasted grain and more sweet citrus accumulate toward the midpalate, like charred sourdough bread topped with orange marmalade or apricot jam. It’s a pleasant combo at this point, though a somewhat thin mouthfeel allows the fruit to die back early while bread remains, contributing to a nearly charred character. Flavors continue on their gradually more tannic route, and for six years old, the back palate becomes fairly heavy on leather. The finish layers on most zested citrus, cereal grain, and oak with a smaller thread of lingering sweet breakfast cereal.

100 proof.

B+ / $60

The post Review: La Pulga Tequila (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Tequila continues to take the country by storm but perhaps nowhere more so than in Texas. Three Ft. Worth-based entrepreneurs are getting in on the action with another addition to the growing La Pulga, a tequila distilled and bottled in Jalisco, Mexico but proudly born in “Cowtown.” Or so goes the press release. The name comes from the La Pulga market, one of the oldest open air flea markets in the country and a fixture of Ft. Worth. Notably, the company’s Head of Spirits is Ale Ochoa, a whiskey scientist and Master Blender formerly with Fort Worth-based Firestone & Robertson Distilling Co. Today, we’re looking at two of the brand’s three classic expressions, each of which is distilled from 100% Blue Weber agave and certified additive-free.

Update 2026: We’re adding coverage of La Pulga’s Double Barrel Reposado.

NOM 1068.

La Pulga Tequila Blanco Review

This unaged silver tequila is impressively earthy and green on the nose with big notes of olive brine, clay, and cut grass. As it opens, agave pulp, lime peel, and plantain add some sweetness, but a healthy dash of black pepper keeps things on the savory side. The palate is a touch sweeter than the aroma but still quite rustic and piquant with a rich minerality – sea salt and flint – and notes of fresh agave, dried lime, and cilantro. The finish is peppery and dry with lingering notes of green olive and citrus. 80 proof. B+ / $45 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

La Pulga Tequila Reposado Review

Seven months of aging in ex-bourbon barrels has really subdued the blanco’s aroma, silencing for the most part all of those green and briny notes with a soft, subtle blanket of vanilla icing and cinnamon sugar. As it opens, the agave, classically vegetal and sweet, emerges. The palate is more viscous than the blanco with comparatively lush notes of cinnamon syrup, honey candies, and cooked agave. While sweeter than the blanco, it’s still well-balanced. The midpalate, nicely spiced with clove, cracked pepper, and grated cinnamon, transitions seamlessly to a warming, balanced finish of Red Hots, wintergreen, and vanilla taffy. While the blanco is a bit more interesting, the reposado should be a crowd pleaser. 80 proof. A- / $55 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

La Pulga Tequila Reposado Double Barrel Review

This limited edition reposado takes the standard La Pulga reposado (as above) and gives it a second maturation in fresh Still Austin Red Corn Bourbon barrels. There’s no word on the length of the finishing, but the tequila is bottled at a higher abv, 45%. It’s been several years since I’ve tasted La Pulga’s standard Reposado, but this expression is quite a lively experience and, based on my earlier notes, a significant upgrade. Seductive and rich on the nose, the tequila pops right away with vanilla and cinnamon notes, the underlying agave character an exercise in gentle restraint. Above all, it smells clean and refreshing, immediately inviting. On the palate a rush of vanilla caramel kicks things off, backed up with some bright citrus, almost juicy with orange notes. Baking spice follows but it remains quite gentle, gingery and laced with allspice, complementary to the sweeter notes that kick things off. A final rush of agave reminds you that you’re drinking tequila, not rum, leaving things on a gentle, grassy note. The best I’ve seen from La Pulga to date. 90 proof. A / $70

The post Review: Sapporo Premium Non-Alcoholic Beer appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Also known as Sapporo 0.0%, Sapporo Premium Non-Alcoholic is the N/A version of the Japanese classic, more or less anyway. Unlike a lot of non-alc beers, it doesn’t particularly taste like classic Sapporo, attacking with a very lemon-forward quality that threatens to overwhelm everything before it ever gets going. A spritz of apple cider adds a sweeter fruit element, helping to calm things down at least a little. As the palate develops the beer takes on a distinct maltiness, tempering the earlier fruit notes. Some brown sugar lingers underneath all the grainy notes until a reprise of that zippy lemon returns in time for the finish. It’s certainly a pleasant enough brew, though it feels like the point of all that bright acidity is to cover up the lack of alcohol. Weirdly enough, it works.

B+ / $11 per six-pack
